rmt-2008-team-01.title: Simplify the exponent
rmt-2008-team-01.body:
For $\cos x\ne0$, $\sin x\cos x\tan x=\sin^2x\le1$. So the expression is at most $e^1=e$, and values arbitrarily close to $e$ occur as $x\to\frac\pi2$, so the supremum is $e$ (not attained, since $\tan x$ is undefined at $\frac\pi2$).

**Answer: $e$**

rmt-2008-team-02.title: Vertex of the parabola
rmt-2008-team-02.body:
$56z-4z^2=4z(14-z)$ is a downward parabola with vertex at $z=\frac{56}8=7$, an integer. (Calculus: the derivative $56-8z$ is zero at $z=7$.)

**Answer: 7**

rmt-2008-team-03.title: Find the cycle
rmt-2008-team-03.body:
The terms are $10,5,12,6,3,8,4,2,1,4,2,1,\dots$ From the seventh term on the sequence is $4,2,1$ repeating with period $3$. Terms $7,10,13,\dots$ equal $4$, i.e. terms with index $\equiv1\pmod3$. Since $2008=3\cdot669+1$, the $2008^{\text{th}}$ term is $4$.

**Answer: 4**

rmt-2008-team-05.title: Two pyramids
rmt-2008-team-05.body:
The octahedron consists of two square pyramids. The four vertices around the middle are the centres of the four side faces of the cube; they form a square whose vertices are the midpoints of the sides of the unit square, so its area is $\frac12$. The height of each pyramid is $\frac12$. Each pyramid has volume $\frac13\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac12=\frac1{12}$, so the total is $\frac16$.

**Answer: $\frac16$**

rmt-2008-team-06.title: Cross product
rmt-2008-team-06.body:
Take $\vec u=(-x,y,0)$ and $\vec v=(-x,0,z)$, the vectors from the first vertex to the other two. $\vec u\times\vec v=(yz,\,xz,\,xy)$. The area is half the magnitude: $\frac12\sqrt{y^2z^2+x^2z^2+x^2y^2}$.

**Answer: $\frac12\sqrt{x^2y^2+y^2z^2+z^2x^2}$**

rmt-2008-team-07.title: Set up equations
rmt-2008-team-07.body:
Let $a,b,c,d$ be the four corners of the square, attached to the exits $A,B,C,D$. From a corner she picks one of $3$ directions (the exit, or the two neighbouring corners). Let $p_a,p_b,p_c,p_d$ be the probabilities of eventually exiting at $A$ from each corner. By symmetry $p_b=p_d$. Then

$p_a=\frac13+\frac23p_b$, $p_b=\frac13p_a+\frac13p_c$, $p_c=\frac23p_b$.

Substituting $p_c$: $p_b=\frac13p_a+\frac29p_b$, so $p_b=\frac37p_a$. Then $p_a=\frac13+\frac23\cdot\frac37p_a=\frac13+\frac27p_a$, so $\frac57p_a=\frac13$ and $p_a=\frac7{15}$.

**Answer: $\frac7{15}$**

rmt-2008-team-08.title: Coordinates
rmt-2008-team-08.body:
Put $E=(0,0)$, $P=(1,0)$, $A=\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$ so that $AE=EP=AP=1$. Then $ET=2$, $T=(2,0)$, and $EX=4$, $X=(4,0)$. $\vec{AE}=\left(-\frac12,-\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$, $\vec{AX}=\left(\frac72,-\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$. $\vec{AE}\cdot\vec{AX}=-\frac74+\frac34=-1$, $|AE|=1$, $|AX|=\sqrt{\frac{49}4+\frac34}=\sqrt{13}$. So $\cos\angle XAE=-\frac1{\sqrt{13}}=-\frac{\sqrt{13}}{13}$.

**Answer: $-\frac{\sqrt{13}}{13}$**

rmt-2008-team-09.title: Coordinates
rmt-2008-team-09.body:
Put $X=(0,0)$, $D=(n,0)$ on the $x$-axis (scale so $KJ=1$, so $KC=n=XD$), $K=(0,t)$, $C=(n,t)$, $J=(1,t)$. Line $XJ$: $y=tx$. Line $KD$: $y=t-\frac tnx$. Intersection: $tx=t-\frac tnx$, so $x\left(1+\frac1n\right)=1$ and $x=\frac n{n+1}$. Since $QZ\perp XK$ and $XK$ is vertical, $QZ$ is the horizontal distance $\frac n{n+1}$. So $\frac{XD}{QZ}=\frac{n}{n/(n+1)}=n+1$.

**Answer: $n+1$**

rmt-2008-team-09.title: Similar triangles
rmt-2008-team-09.body:
Since $XD\parallel KJ$, triangles $QXD$ and $QJK$ are similar with ratio $XD:KJ=KC:KJ=n$, so $QD:QK=n:1$ and $\frac{KQ}{KD}=\frac1{n+1}$. Also $QZ\parallel XD$ (both are perpendicular to $XK$), so triangles $KZQ$ and $KXD$ are similar and $\frac{QZ}{XD}=\frac{KQ}{KD}=\frac1{n+1}$. Hence $\frac{XD}{QZ}=n+1$.

**Answer: $n+1$**

rmt-2008-team-10.title: Classes from A and B
rmt-2008-team-10.body:
Cards $A$ and $B$ alone split the numbers into four classes: on both ($2,7$), on $A$ only ($3,5$), on $B$ only ($4,6$), on neither ($1,8$). The new card must separate the two numbers of every class, so it must contain exactly one number from each class: $2^4=16$ choices out of $\binom84=70$. The probability is $\frac{16}{70}=\frac8{35}$.

**Answer: $\frac8{35}$**

rmt-2008-team-12.title: Count parallel chord pairs
rmt-2008-team-12.body:
Label the vertices $0,\dots,7$. Chords $\{i,j\}$ are parallel exactly when they have the same value of $i+j\pmod8$. For even sums there are $3$ chords, for odd sums $4$ chords, so there are $4\binom32+4\binom42=12+24=36$ pairs of parallel chords. Each pair determines a quadrilateral having these chords as opposite sides, and it is a rectangle exactly when it has two pairs of parallel sides, which happens for $\binom42=6$ rectangles (counted twice). So there are $36-6=30$ distinct quadrilaterals with a pair of parallel sides, of which $6$ are rectangles: $24$ nonrectangular trapezoids.

**Answer: 24**

rmt-2008-team-12.title: By shape
rmt-2008-team-12.body:
The trapezoids are of three types, each with $8$ rotations: $ABCD$ (three consecutive sides), $ACDF$, and $ABDE$. That is $3\cdot8=24$.

**Answer: 24**

rmt-2008-team-13.title: Roots of x^9 + 1
rmt-2008-team-13.body:
The polynomial equals $\frac{x^9+1}{x+1}$. So its roots are the $9$th roots of $-1$ other than $x=-1$. Those have $r=1$ and $9\theta=180+360k$, i.e. $\theta=20+40k$ degrees: $20,60,100,140,180,220,260,300,340$. Removing $180$ (the root $x=-1$) leaves $20,60,100,140,220,260,300,340$.

**Answer: $20^\circ,60^\circ,100^\circ,140^\circ,220^\circ,260^\circ,300^\circ,340^\circ$**

rmt-2008-team-14.title: Substitute u = tan x
rmt-2008-team-14.body:
With $u=\tan x$, $dx=\frac{du}{1+u^2}$ and the integral becomes $\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{u^n}{1+u^2}\,du$ (with $|u|^n$ for $u<0$). For large $|u|$ the integrand behaves like $|u|^{n-2}$, which is integrable at infinity iff $n-2<-1$, i.e. $n<1$ (for $n=1$ it behaves like $\frac1u$ and diverges). Near $u=0$ it behaves like $|u|^n$, integrable iff $n>-1$. So the integral is defined exactly for $-1<n<1$.

**Answer: $-1<n<1$**

rmt-2008-team-15.title: Solve for crossings
rmt-2008-team-15.body:
Two parameter values $t_1<t_2$ give the same point iff $\sin t_1=\sin t_2$ and $\cos t_1+\frac{t_1}2=\cos t_2+\frac{t_2}2$. Equal sines with $t_2\ne t_1+2\pi k$ give $t_2=\pi-t_1+2\pi k$ (if $t_2=t_1+2\pi k$ the $x$-coordinates differ by $\pi k\ne0$). Then $\cos t_2=-\cos t_1$ and the $x$-equation becomes $-2\cos t_1+\frac{\pi}2-t_1+\pi k=0$. For each $k$ this has a solution, and they occur at $x$-values spaced about $\pi$ apart: the first at $x\approx3.93$, then $7.07,10.21,\dots$. The ones with $1\le x\le40$ are at $x\approx3.93+3.14j$ for $j=0,\dots,11$ (the next, about $41.6$, is out of range). A numerical check confirms $12$ crossings.

**Answer: 12**
